passage: With the school bus leaving in ten minutes and rain drumming on the tin roof, the class hunted for the missing lab register. Mehak watched Swati, who stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor. "She's hiding something," Mehak whispered to her bench-mate. "Look, she won't even look at Ma'am." Meanwhile Rudra, who had been the last to use the register, answered every question with an easy smile. The teacher asked everyone to check their bags anyway. The register slid out of Rudra's folder. He shrugged. "Must have picked it up by mistake." Mehak felt her cheeks burn. On the bus she sat beside Swati, who admitted she always went stiff when a teacher asked questions, even when she had done nothing. Mehak stared at the wet window, thinking how sure she had felt, and how wrong.

qa.q: What was Swati doing while the class searched for the register?
qa.a: Swati stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when the register slid out of Rudra's folder?
qa.a: Mehak felt embarrassed and ashamed of her quick judgement; her cheeks burned because she had been so sure Swati's fidgeting meant guilt.

qa.q: What could Mehak do next time she is tempted to read guilt from someone's body language?
qa.a: She could remind herself that nervousness is not proof, wait for facts such as who last used the register, and keep her guess to herself instead of whispering it.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati when classmates read her stiffness as guilt?
qa.a: Swati goes stiff whenever a teacher asks questions, even when she has done nothing, so being suspected for it would feel unfair and make her even more tense.

grounding: Shows an observer who takes fidgeting and avoided eye contact as proof of lying, then sees that the nervous classmate was innocent while the calm one had the missing register.

passage:
Monday: The visitor at the news desk told his story without a single pause: a relief drive after the floods, three hundred families fed, photos on his phone. Abhinav felt his chest warm; the man seemed so sincere. Afreen, the desk editor, only asked, "Registration papers? Names we can call?"
Wednesday: Abhinav laid his notes side by side. On Monday the drive had begun in August; in the man's follow-up email it began in July. The trust number he gave did not appear in the state register. Abhinav phoned the panchayat office of the village named, and the clerk said no such drive had come through.
The next Monday: Abhinav pinned a card above his desk: dates, documents, one independent voice. When a new intern gushed about a "really genuine" caller, Abhinav smiled. "The smoothest tellers are sometimes the most rehearsed. Let's check."

qa.q: Which month did the man's follow-up email give for the start of the drive?
qa.a: The man's follow-up email said the drive began in July, though on Monday it had begun in August.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel while hearing the visitor's story on Monday?
qa.a: Abhinav felt warm and trusting; the story was fluent and moving, and the man seemed so sincere.

qa.q: Which checks worked, and why?
qa.a: Comparing dates across tellings, searching the state register and calling the panchayat office tested the claim against independent sources instead of the man's confident manner.

qa.q: How might a genuine relief volunteer see the desk's checks?
qa.a: A genuine volunteer would likely have papers and contacts ready and might welcome the checks, since verified coverage makes their work more believable.

grounding: Shows an adult learning to test claims through consistent dates, records and an independent call rather than a gut sense of the speaker's sincerity.

passage: You know me, Varun, I'm not a suspicious person. At the clinic front desk I believe people all day. Someone says they're here for their mother's report, I take them at their word and point them to the lab. Most people are just people. But last month a man walked in, very polite, said he was from an insurance office and needed copies of five patients' files, "urgently, today." Something shifted in me. Not accusation; I didn't call him a fraud. I only said, "Of course. Send the request on your office letterhead to our records officer and it will be processed." He said he'd come back. He never did. I still don't know if he was a fraud. Maybe he was just in a hurry. But patient files aren't a pen someone borrows. So that's Rehana's rule now: easy trust for small things, papers for big ones.

qa.q: What did the man ask for at the clinic front desk?
qa.a: He said he was from an insurance office and needed copies of five patients' files, urgently, today.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when the man pressed for the files?
qa.a: Rehana felt a quiet wariness, as if something shifted, yet stayed calm and did not feel sure enough to accuse him.

qa.q: Why was asking for a letter to the records officer a wise step?
qa.a: It raised the standard of proof to match the high stakes without calling the man a liar, and sent the request through an official channel he could not skip.

qa.q: How might a patient whose file was requested see Rehana's caution?
qa.a: A patient would likely feel protected and grateful that private records were not handed over just because a stranger sounded polite and urgent.

grounding: Shows a person who trusts by default in small matters but asks for stronger proof when the stakes rise, without accusing anyone.

passage: In the school library in Melbourne, Tuan rehearsed under his breath before Nour, the Year 12 captain of the debate team, came in. Trials for the last spot were on Friday. "Your speech at assembly was honestly the best thing I've heard all year," he said, sliding into the seat beside her. He hadn't actually listened to most of it. He praised her notes, her shoes, the way she ran meetings. Nour smiled, then asked, "Which part of the speech did you like?" Tuan's mind went blank. "Uh, all of it?" She nodded slowly and went back to her notes. Walking home past the tram stop, Tuan kept replaying that pause. He had wanted her vote, not her speech, and she had probably felt the difference. He decided to turn up on Friday with his best argument instead.

qa.q: When were trials for the last spot on the debate team?
qa.a: Trials for the last spot were on Friday.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when Nour asked which part of the speech he liked?
qa.a: Tuan felt caught and embarrassed, because he hadn't listened to most of the speech and his praise was aimed at winning her vote.

qa.q: What could Tuan try instead of heaping on compliments?
qa.a: He could earn the spot with his own argument at trials, and keep praise for moments when he means something specific.

qa.q: How might Nour see Tuan's compliments after that pause?
qa.a: Nour may sense the praise was empty and aimed at the trial, which could make her trust his later compliments less.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager heaping compliments on an older student to win a team place, with the praise aimed at an outcome rather than at her.

subtype: Learning to tell warmth from steering [Response]
passage: In the girls' hostel common room, Sharmila read her short story aloud before sending it to the inter-school contest. "It's perfect, don't change a word," said Pallavi at once, and then, "Can I borrow your chemistry journal tonight?" Noor had listened with her chin in her hand. "The opening is lovely, the bit with the rain," she said. "But the ending rushes. I didn't believe the sister forgave so fast." Sharmila's face went hot. She wanted to argue. That night, lying awake, she reread the ending. Noor was right; it did rush. And she noticed something else: Pallavi's praise always seemed to arrive with a request, while Noor asked for nothing. Next morning she knocked on Noor's door with two cups of tea and a new draft. "Will you read it again? Be honest."

qa.q: Which part of the story did Noor call lovely?
qa.a: Noor said the opening was lovely, the bit with the rain.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Noor criticised the ending?
qa.a: Sharmila felt stung and defensive; her face went hot and she wanted to argue before she reread it.

qa.q: What did Sharmila learn to look for in a friend's feedback?
qa.a: She learned to notice whether praise arrives with a request; a friend like Noor, who praises specific parts, disagrees honestly and asks nothing back, is more trustworthy.

qa.q: What might it be like for Noor to give honest criticism?
qa.a: Noor risks upsetting a friend, so it may feel uncomfortable, but being asked to read again shows her honesty is valued.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that a friend who praises and also disagrees is more trustworthy than one whose praise comes with requests.

passage: The dust had just settled from the evening bus when Kiran walked into the little agri-shop in the kasba with a box of sweets. "Vijay-ji, the whole block talks about you," he said. "So young and running this shop better than men twice your age. Farmers trust only you." Vijay felt his ears warm. Nobody had called him Vijay-ji before. Kiran spread out glossy leaflets for a new seed variety and a stock agreement. "For a smart man like you, it's just a signature." Vijay picked up the pen. Questions rose in his mind about trials and which farmers had used it, but asking felt rude after such kindness. Then his father's old diary on the counter caught his eye, full of crossed-out company names. Vijay put the pen down. "Leave the papers. I'll read them with Bapu tonight." Kiran's smile tightened for a second.

qa.q: What did Kiran bring when he walked into the shop?
qa.a: Kiran brought a box of sweets.

qa.q: Why did asking questions feel hard for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay felt flattered and warm at being called Vijay-ji, so questioning Kiran felt rude and awkward after such kindness.

qa.q: What protective step did Vijay take, and why does it help?
qa.a: He put the pen down and kept the papers to read with Bapu that night, which gave him time and a second person away from the praise.

qa.q: What might Kiran's tightened smile suggest about how he sees the delay?
qa.a: It may suggest Kiran was counting on a quick signature and saw the pause as a setback, though a smile alone cannot prove what he intended.

grounding: Shows a young shopkeeper whose guard drops under lavish praise from someone who wants a signature, making questions feel rude.

subtype: Spotting the ask behind the praise [Observer]
passage:
Hi Jagdish,
Remember how you warned me that offices have their own weather? I think I've found a pattern. There's a team lead here, Sethi, who is lovely to everyone. On Monday he told Farah her slides were "world class," and ten minutes later asked her to cover his client call. On Wednesday he called our intern "the future of this company" right before handing him a pile of scanning. Today it was my turn: "You're the only one who writes clean reports." Then: "Could you finish my quarterly summary by Friday?"
The compliment was vague, nothing about which report. When you praised my work last year, you mentioned the chart on page three. That felt different.
I said I'd check my deadlines and reply tomorrow. I'm going to say no.
Hope Pune is treating you well.
Ankita

qa.q: What did Sethi ask Farah to do after praising her slides?
qa.a: Ten minutes later he asked her to cover his client call.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel about Sethi's compliment today?
qa.a: Ankita feels wary and unconvinced, because the praise was vague and came just before a request, so it seemed aimed at a yes.

qa.q: What makes Ankita's reply a sensible step?
qa.a: Saying the answer would come tomorrow after checking deadlines separates the decision from the flattery and lets the request be judged on its own.

qa.q: How might the intern see Sethi's praise?
qa.a: The intern may feel pleased at first to be called the future of the company, then feel used when the praise turns out to be a lead-in to scanning.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that vague compliments arrive just before requests, unlike specific praise that does not depend on a yes.

passage: People ask me how you say no to someone who's being so nice. Honestly, I don't always. But here's what happened in spring. My cousin Jatin came to the shop and said the most beautiful things: that my blouses were the best stitching in Nagpur, that I had an eye no one else had. I felt ten feet tall. I said, "Thank you, Jatin, that means a lot," and I meant it. Then he asked if my two tailors could work at his wedding-season stall for three weekends. My instinct was to say yes on the spot, because no felt like throwing his kindness back at him. Instead I said, "Let me look at my orders and call you Thursday." On Thursday the orders said no. So I told him no, warmly. He sulked a bit, but we're fine. I'm Kalyani, and that's my trick: enjoy the praise tonight, decide the favour tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Jatin ask of Kalyani's tailors?
qa.a: He asked if the two tailors could work at his wedding-season stall for three weekends.

qa.q: Why was Kalyani tempted to say yes on the spot?
qa.a: Kalyani felt proud and touched by the praise, and refusing felt like throwing Jatin's kindness back at him.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who gets lavish praise followed by a favour?
qa.a: Thank the person sincerely, then set a time to decide, as Kalyani did by checking the orders before calling back on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when the answer is no?
qa.a: Jatin may feel disappointed and a bit sulky, but because the no came warmly and after real checking, the relationship stayed fine.

grounding: Shows a person who enjoys a kind word, waits before deciding, and judges the favour on its merits.

passage:
Day 2: Charu had met Pranav at the college film club only on Saturday, but by Monday she had sent him forty messages, a playlist titled "Us", and a photo of two train tickets to Shimla "for our first trip". Her new hostel room was so quiet at night; his replies made it feel full.
Day 5: She turned up at his lab with lunch, a handmade card and a promise: "I've never felt this with anyone. We're forever." Pranav laughed awkwardly and said he had a group project. Charu's stomach dropped. She texted him eleven times that evening.
Day 12: Pranav asked to slow down. Charu cried, then called her school friend Leena, who asked gently, "Do you even know his favourite food?" Charu didn't. She sat with that for a long time, and admitted how lonely her first weeks in the city had been.

qa.q: What was the playlist Charu sent called?
qa.a: The playlist was titled Us.

qa.q: Why did Charu keep flooding Pranav with messages?
qa.a: Charu felt lonely in her quiet new hostel room, and Pranav's replies made it feel full, so she clung anxiously to the new bond.

qa.q: What small step could help Charu the next time she feels a rush like this?
qa.a: She could let a new bond grow at a normal pace, keep leaning on friends like Leena, and treat the speed itself as a sign she is racing ahead of knowing the person.

qa.q: What is it like for Pranav to hear promises of forever within a week?
qa.a: Pranav seems uncomfortable and overwhelmed; he laughs awkwardly, points to his project, and finally asks to slow down.

grounding: Shows a lonely young adult flooding a new acquaintance with messages, plans and promises of forever within days, where the speed is the warning sign.
